Which rentals Ohio landlord-tenant law covers

Chapter 5321 of the Revised Code governs residential rentals across Ohio, and R.C. 5321.01 defines the terms. A tenant is someone entitled under a rental agreement to use and occupy residential premises to the exclusion of others. A landlord can be the owner, lessor or sublessor, an agent, or anyone authorized to manage the premises or collect rent. A rental agreement can be written or oral.

Several kinds of occupancy fall outside the chapter: hospitals and care homes, hotels, motels and similar transient lodging, boarding school housing, farm residences tied to renting at least two acres of farmland, and an owner living in a condominium unit. If you are selling a house that is rented out, confirm the arrangement is a true residential tenancy before you lean on the chapter's rules.

The chapter also removes local control of rents. Under R.C. 5321.19, no city, county or township may impose rent control or rent stabilization or otherwise regulate rights and obligations the chapter already covers. Local building, housing, health and safety codes stay in force, and so do rent rules for housing the local government itself owns.

Keeping a rental fit to live in

The landlord's duties are listed in R.C. 5321.04. A landlord who is party to a rental agreement must:

  • Follow building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety.
  • Repair what is broken and do whatever is reasonably needed to keep the unit livable.
  • Keep common areas safe and sanitary.
  • Keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air conditioning fixtures and appliances that the landlord supplies in good working order.
  • Supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat, unless the building is not required to have them or the tenant controls the system.
  • Provide waste receptacles and removal when the landlord has agreements covering four or more units in one structure.

Entry has its own rule. Except in an emergency or when notice is impracticable, the landlord gives reasonable notice and enters at reasonable times, and twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable. A landlord who enters improperly, or demands entry so often that it harasses the tenant, can owe the tenant proven losses and legal fees, and the tenant may seek an injunction or walk away from the agreement.

If you own a rental in poor shape, fix code problems before you list. A tenant can use these remedies before the sale closes.

Security deposits

The deposit rules are in R.C. 5321.16. The part of a deposit above fifty dollars or one month's periodic rent, whichever is greater, earns five percent annual interest if the tenant stays six months or more. The landlord figures and pays that interest once a year.

When the tenancy ends, the landlord may apply the deposit to past due rent and to damages caused by the tenant's breach of the rental agreement or of the tenant's statutory duties. Every deduction must be itemized in a written notice delivered with the amount owed, within a month of the day the agreement ends and the keys come back.

The tenant has a job too: give the landlord a forwarding address in writing. Without one, the tenant cannot collect damages or attorney's fees if the deposit is mishandled. If the landlord does fail to comply, the tenant may recover the money due, damages equal to the amount wrongfully withheld, and reasonable attorney's fees.

Notice to end a tenancy versus notice to start an eviction

Ending a periodic tenancy and starting an eviction are separate steps. Under R.C. 5321.17, either side can end a weekly rental on a week's notice, and a rental that renews monthly on notice that reaches the other side a full thirty days ahead.

An eviction action under Chapter 1923 begins with a different notice. R.C. 1923.04 requires the party seeking possession to tell the other to leave three or more days before filing. The notice goes by certified mail with return receipt, by a written copy handed to the defendant, or by a copy left at the usual home or the premises. A landlord's notice must carry this wording, printed or written conspicuously: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance."

One narrow case moves faster. If a landlord has actual knowledge or reasonable cause to believe a tenant or household member has engaged in a violation described in R.C. 1923.02(A)(6)(a)(i), the landlord gives a three-day termination notice and then promptly files an action under Chapter 1923 if the tenant stays.

Repairs, retaliation and lockouts

Three protections come up most often.

  • Repairs. Under R.C. 5321.07, a tenant sends written notice naming the problem to the place rent is normally paid. When the problem outlasts a reasonable time or thirty days, whichever comes first, and rent is paid up, the tenant may pay rent into the municipal or county court, petition for a repair order, or terminate the agreement.
  • Retaliation. Under R.C. 5321.02, a landlord cannot raise rent, trim services, or file or threaten an eviction because a tenant reported a code violation to a government agency, made a habitability complaint to the landlord, or bargained collectively with other tenants.
  • Self-help. Under R.C. 5321.15, a landlord may not cut off utilities, lock a tenant out, or threaten unlawful acts to recover possession, and may not seize a tenant's belongings for rent without a court order. A landlord who does so owes all damages caused plus attorney's fees.

Landlords whose agreements cover three or fewer dwelling units, and who said so in writing, are outside the rent-deposit remedy, as are student tenants in college-owned housing. A small landlord should check that exception before assuming it applies.

Deadlines to check before selling a rental

Landlord and tenant periods in the Ohio Revised Code
SubjectPeriod or amount
Deposit itemization and refund (5321.16(B))One month from the end of the agreement and handover of possession
Interest on large deposits (5321.16(A))Five percent annually on the part above $50 or one month's rent, once the tenant has stayed six months
Ending a monthly rental (5321.17(B))Thirty days before rent is next due
Ending a weekly rental (5321.17(A))A week's notice
Notice to leave before an eviction filing (1923.04(A))3 or more days
Entry notice presumed reasonable (5321.04(A)(8))24 hours
Repair cure window before tenant remedies (5321.07(B))Reasonable time or 30 days, whichever is sooner

Before listing a tenant-occupied house, gather the written lease, the rent ledger and the deposit records. Then ask the closing agent how the lease and the held deposit pass to a buyer. Some owners tired of repairs and turnover choose a direct as-is cash purchase while a tenant lives in the house, which removes the repair list and the showings from the picture.

Frequently asked questions

What notice ends a monthly rental in Ohio?

Thirty days before rent is next due. A weekly rental needs seven days before the date it ends. R.C. 5321.17 sets both periods.

When must a deposit come back to an Ohio tenant?

Within thirty days of the day the lease ends and the tenant hands the unit back. Itemized deductions go in writing with the balance. A tenant who wants the refund mailed should give a forwarding address in writing.

Can an Ohio landlord enter without permission?

Only with reasonable notice and at reasonable times, except in an emergency or when notice is impracticable. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice.

Can Ohio cities set rent control?

No. R.C. 5321.19 bars political subdivisions from rent control or rent stabilization on private rentals the chapter regulates. Local housing and building codes still apply.

Can an Ohio landlord lock a tenant out over unpaid rent?

No. R.C. 5321.15 prohibits cutting off utilities, excluding a tenant from the premises, and threatening unlawful acts to recover possession outside Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. The landlord is liable for damages and attorney's fees.

How many days of notice before an Ohio eviction?

At least three in most cases. Before filing in court, R.C. 1923.04 has the party seeking possession tell the other side to leave, at least three days ahead. Three delivery methods work: certified mail with return receipt requested, a written copy handed over in person, or a copy left at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises.

When a landlord is recovering a residence, the notice must carry this statement in a conspicuous place: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." Check for that language first, whether you are the owner or a buyer reviewing the file.

Notice periods that end a tenancy

The three-day notice opens the door to court, but other chapters of the Revised Code set the notice that ends the tenancy to begin with. The table covers the ones that come up most when a rented house is being sold.

Ohio notice periods for ending a residential tenancy
SituationNotice required
Week-to-week tenancy (R.C. 5321.17(A))At least seven days before the termination date
Month-to-month tenancy (R.C. 5321.17(B))At least thirty days before the periodic rental date
Tenant fails a health and safety duty (R.C. 5321.11)Written notice, ending not less than thirty days after receipt
Drug-related violation tied to the premises (R.C. 5321.17(C))Termination three days after the notice is given
Land installment contract (R.C. 1923.04(B))Notice under R.C. 5313.06 counts as the notice to leave

Notice when the tenant is behind on rent

Under R.C. 1923.02(B), a tenant on an oral tenancy who defaults on rent forfeits the right to occupy, and the landlord can end the tenancy with the three-day notice from R.C. 1923.04. Staying past the end of the term, or breaching a written rental agreement, also exposes a tenant to suit after that notice period.

Record how and when you delivered it. Clerks and judges look at the delivery method, so be ready to show the certified mail receipt, the date of hand delivery, or where a copy was left.

Special cases with their own delivery rules

A few situations carry separate delivery steps. When the person to be removed is a deceased resident of a manufactured home park, R.C. 1923.04(C) calls for leaving the notice at the premises and also mailing it by ordinary mail to the executor or administrator if the probate court has appointed one, and to the resident's spouse and other immediate family members whose names and addresses the park operator knows.

Student tenants of a college or university follow a separate path under R.C. 5321.031, which the eviction chapter points to. An owner with a unit of that type should read that section before serving anything.

What a landlord may not do instead of giving notice

Ohio bars self-help eviction. R.C. 5321.15 forbids a landlord from cutting off utilities or services, locking the tenant out, or threatening an unlawful act to recover possession, except through the court process in Chapters 1923, 5303 and 5321. It also bars seizing a tenant's furnishings or possessions to collect rent without a court order. A landlord who breaks the rule owes the tenant all damages plus reasonable attorney fees.

R.C. 5321.02 adds a retaliation rule. A landlord cannot raise rent, reduce services, or file or threaten a possession action because the tenant:

  • reported a building, housing, health or safety code violation that materially affects health and safety to a government agency;
  • complained to the landlord about a violation of the landlord's duties under R.C. 5321.04;
  • joined other tenants to negotiate collectively over the rental agreement.

Retaliation works as a defense in the possession case. The tenant may also recover possession or end the agreement, and collect actual damages and attorney fees. A rent increase that reflects the cost of improvements the landlord installed is allowed.

How a notice affects a sale

The notice decides whether the buyer gets an empty house or one with a tenant in it. An owner who wants a vacant house should serve the right notice for the tenancy type, such as thirty days for a month-to-month tenant, then follow the court steps if the tenant stays. A buyer who is happy to keep the tenant can skip the notice and take over the lease.

Security deposits matter at closing and at move-out. R.C. 5321.16 says the part of a deposit that exceeds fifty dollars or one month's rent, whichever is larger, earns five percent a year when the tenant stays six months or more. When the tenancy ends, the landlord itemizes any deductions in writing within thirty days after termination and delivery of possession. The tenant has to provide a forwarding address. A landlord who wrongly withholds owes the withheld amount again as damages plus attorney fees.

Before listing a rented house, sort the tenancy into a type, because the type picks the notice. Write down the rental period, the rent ledger, how the tenant was told to leave and on what date. If a buyer asks, you can then show exactly where the process stands, which keeps a contract from stalling over missing paperwork. Where possible, agree on a move-out date in writing with the tenant, since a signed agreement avoids the court calendar altogether.

  • Pull the lease, ledger and any notices before listing.
  • Tell the title company where the deposit sits.
  • Decide in the contract whether the buyer takes the house vacant or tenant-occupied.

Some cash buyers will take the house with the tenant still inside, or wait while you finish the notice process, since no lender is demanding vacant possession at closing.

Getting help with a notice

A plain-language timeline for tenants starts with the three-day notice: read the notice for the required sentences, try to settle before a case is filed, and put any agreement in writing. Free legal services are available to some low-income tenants through Right to Counsel programs in Akron, Cleveland, Columbus and Toledo, and through local legal aid offices elsewhere.

After the notice period runs out, a landlord can ask the municipal or county court clerk for the rental address how to file. Clerks explain forms and fees but do not give legal advice. Owners with a complicated tenancy, such as a lease with a purchase option or a mixed-use building, should speak with a landlord attorney before serving anything.

Frequently asked questions

Is a three-day notice in Ohio an eviction?

No. It is the required warning before a case. R.C. 1923.04 says the notice must be given three or more days before the court action begins, and only a court judgment can lead to removal by an officer.

Can an Ohio landlord change the locks or shut off the water to force a tenant out?

No. R.C. 5321.15 forbids terminating utilities or services, excluding the tenant, or threatening unlawful acts to recover possession. The landlord owes damages and attorney fees for a violation.

What notice ends a month-to-month Ohio tenancy?

At least thirty days before the periodic rental date, under R.C. 5321.17(B). For a week-to-week tenancy, the minimum is seven days before the termination date.

Does the Ohio eviction notice have to say anything specific?

Yes. A residential notice under R.C. 1923.04 must contain the statutory statement that begins 'You are being asked to leave the premises.' It must be printed or written conspicuously.

Can I sell my rented Ohio house while a notice is pending?

Yes, an owner can contract to sell, but the tenant's right to remain follows the notice and court process. Settle in the contract who delivers possession and when, and keep copies of every notice for the buyer.
